headline: Epilepsy Drug Shows Promise in Reversing Joint Damage
meta_description: Yale researchers found that lacosamide, an FDA-approved epilepsy medication, may reverse cartilage damage in osteoarthritis while reducing pain.
summary_short: Researchers at Yale discovered that an existing epilepsy drug could do more than ease osteoarthritis pain—it may actually reverse the underlying joint damage.
body:
For millions of people living with osteoarthritis, pain and stiffness make everyday life progressively harder. Most treatments on the market reduce symptoms temporarily but fail to stop the actual destruction of joint tissue. Now, researchers at Yale School of Medicine have identified a fundamentally different approach: repurposing an existing epilepsy drug to not only quiet pain but actively repair damaged cartilage. The medication, lacosamide, appears to block a protein called Nav1.7 that drives both pain signaling and cartilage breakdown. In preclinical studies, when delivered directly into the joint using a specialized hydrogel, the effects were particularly strong. As Charles W. Ohse Professor of Orthopaedics & Rehabilitation Chuan-Ju Liu notes, "We need therapies that don't just mask pain but actually change how the disease progresses."

The discovery hinges on understanding how osteoarthritis actually damages joints. Healthy cartilage relies on a delicate balance: chondrocytes—specialized cells—continuously create new tissue while removing old material. Osteoarthritis disrupts this equilibrium, causing cartilage to break down faster than it regenerates. Nav1.7, long known mainly for its role in pain-signaling nerves, is also highly active in chondrocytes. When osteoarthritis develops, Nav1.7 activity spikes, intensifying both pain and tissue destruction.

What makes this finding remarkable is that lacosamide appears to restore balance at remarkably low doses. At the optimal concentration, the drug encourages cartilage-building proteins while suppressing breakdown processes. It also stimulates release of two beneficial signaling molecules—HSP70 and midkine—that create supportive conditions throughout the joint tissue. The approach avoids relying on opioids while addressing what has been a major gap in treatment: no currently FDA-approved drug stops osteoarthritis pain while preventing structural damage. Liu's team published their findings in Bioactive Materials in October 2026.
quick_facts: Yale researchers repurposed lacosamide, already FDA-approved for epilepsy
Nav1.7 protein drives both pain and cartilage breakdown in osteoarthritis
Drug delivered via specialized hydrogel directly into affected joints
Optimal low dose showed better results than higher concentrations
HSP70 and midkine proteins help restore cartilage repair processes
